parsed.title: Inside Kimsuky’s CHM Tradecraft: Multi-Stage Execution and Selective Payload Delivery
parsed.summary: Kimsuky (APT43) uses a Korean-language Review.chm lure, themed on North Korean food-crisis material, to start a multi-stage infection chain. The CHM launches hidden PowerShell and certutil to decode a VBScript bootstrap, which fetches a reconnaissance stage that profiles the host, lists directories and processes, and uploads the inventory to the C2. The stage also creates a hidden hourly "Edge Updater" scheduled task that retrieves a VBScript handoff into PowerShell. The final PowerShell endpoint returned an empty body during controlled replay, so the operational payload was not recovered. Defenders should treat an empty response as a possible server-side gate rather than an inactive chain.

parsed.title: Mustang Panda targets India's government and energy sectors with ZOHOMURK and MINIRECON
parsed.summary: Acronis TRU attributes two espionage campaigns targeting Indian government entities and the hydropower sector to Mustang Panda, with high confidence. The campaigns use spear-phishing archives containing hidden DLLs that sideload through a legitimate signed executable, delivering a new loader called SHARDLOADER. SHARDLOADER deploys MINIRECON, a WebSocket-based variant of the Toneshell family, or ZOHOMURK, a new implant that uses Zoho WorkDrive for command-and-control and exfiltration. Lures were themed around cooperation agreements between Indian and Taiwanese institutions. Active beaconing from compromised Indian government systems was observed in June 2026, and TRU worked with CERT-In on victim notification. Defenders should watch for non-browser traffic to Zoho WorkDrive and OAuth endpoints, along with the listed persistence keys and scheduled tasks.

parsed.title: Klue Supply Chain Compromise and CRM Data Exfiltration Incident Advisory
parsed.summary: A software supply chain attack against the market intelligence platform Klue allowed a threat actor to access customer integrations and exfiltrate data from downstream SaaS applications, including CRM systems. The intrusion began when a long-unused but still active credential was used to access Klue's backend, where malicious code was deployed to covertly harvest customer OAuth tokens. The stolen tokens were then used to authenticate against connected services such as Salesforce, where records were extracted through API queries at scale. Affected organizations include Huntress and other Klue customers, with exposed data mainly consisting of sales and CRM information. Defenders should revoke and rotate OAuth tokens, review API logs for bulk queries and Python-based user agents, and audit inactive integrations.

parsed.title: The Gentlemen are knocking: сustom backdoors and evolving tactics
parsed.summary: The Gentlemen is a ransomware-as-a-service group that began ramping up activity in early 2026 and ranks among the top 10 ransomware actors by data leak site victim announcements in the first half of 2026. Its affiliates often gain access through internet-exposed hardware VPNs and firewalls using stolen, weak, or default credentials, and may work with initial access brokers. Before deploying ransomware, the group performs internal reconnaissance, uses netsh to capture network traffic, and disables security products, including through bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver (BYOVD) techniques. It spreads the ransomware via Group Policy, NETLOGON, and PsExec, and it also uses a Go-based backdoor that enables remote command execution and SOCKS proxying. Targets span manufacturing, IT services, healthcare, financial services, construction, and logistics, with Brazil, China, Indonesia, Taiwan, and Thailand most heavily affected. Defenders are advised to prioritize vulnerability management and system hardening.

parsed.title: Chrome and Firefox Extensions Posing as Free VPNs Add Clipboard Stealers via Malicious Updates
parsed.summary: Malicious Chrome and Firefox extensions posing as "VPN Go: Free VPN" added clipboard-stealing code through staged updates while retaining visible proxy functionality. The Chrome extension began exfiltrating clipboard data in version 1.1, and the Firefox extension did so starting in version 1.3.3. Both monitor copied text, split it into chunks, and send it to threat actor-controlled HTTP endpoints. The privacy policy and store listings claim no data collection, which the code contradicts. Defenders should treat secrets copied while the extensions were active as exposed, remove them, and scrutinize any update that adds clipboardRead permission.

parsed.title: Chromium extension uses AI‑related branding to redirect browser search
parsed.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence found a malicious Chromium extension named "Search for perplexity ai" that impersonates the Perplexity AI answer engine to lure users into installing it. The extension overrides the default search provider and routes every query, and every real-time search suggestion typed into the Omnibox, through a typosquatted intermediary domain before redirecting users to legitimate search engines. Microsoft assesses the main objective as search traffic interception and data collection, and its server-side code logs full request headers and source IP addresses. The extension uses declarativeNetRequest permissions that are not consistent with a legitimate AI search assistant. Google removed the extension after responsible disclosure, and defenders should restrict untrusted extension installs and monitor for unauthorized search setting changes.

parsed.title: From Bing Search to Ransomware: Bumblebee and AdaptixC2 Deliver Akira
parsed.summary: BumbleBee loader was delivered through SEO poisoning, using a lookalike site and a trojanized ManageEngine OpManager MSI installer that side-loaded the malware via consent.exe. The intrusion was tied to a broader BumbleBee campaign that impersonated multiple enterprise tools, and a related Swisscom-observed intrusion involved the same campaign. The threat actor deployed AdaptixC2, moved laterally over RDP and reverse SSH tunnels, created backup domain admin accounts, and dumped NTDS.dit and LSASS memory. They exfiltrated over 75GB via FileZilla and SFTP to an external server before deploying Akira ransomware about 44 hours after initial access. Defenders should prioritize monitoring for SEO-poisoned software downloads and for suspicious DLL side-loading and reverse SSH tunnels.
